Filippo A. E. Nuccio said:

Is the declaration mainly meant to be signed by individuals or by entities (or both, but then in a structured way according to who is signing or not)?

I believe the website says that only individuals can sign; organisations can endorse though

I unequivocally support the Leiden Declaration. As a former AMS VP, current Editor-in-Chief, and someone bridging academia and industry, I see its message as urgent. AI will shape mathematics. We must uphold rigor, transparency, attribution, and culture. I'm almost never on this site, but this moment is important.

I would like to say that I am very disappointed that, while recognizing that the threats associated to AI "disproportionately affect students and early-career mathematicians", the declaration doesn't make any concrete advice related to this.

I would have expected at the very least something along the lines of:

  • Students have the right to human teaching and supervision of their work
  • Students should not, in any case, feel pressured to use AI tools, nor should we expect their productivity to be higher thanks to / to compete with these tools.

I think this is a critical blind spot, and one more instance of established researchers deciding about the future of mathematics with little care for future mathematicians.

I also found the framing around formalization a bit of a mixed bag. I think that

... formalizations, where the difficulty lies in the translation between computer-encoded and human presentations of concepts

and

... formalized proofs can be checked automatically, without the need for human oversight.

are oversimplifications that pass over how much of a human endeavor formalization is.

Chris Henson said:

...are oversimplifications that pass over how much of a human endeavor formalization is...

Case in point when formalisation is not treated as a proper research artefact requiring human effort and review : https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03194
To be fair, I'm not bothered or angered by the recent announcements on Navier–Stokes and Hodge... https://bsky.app/profile/parclytaxel.art/post/3mv54oxug522i

Sincerely, even if I agree with some things this declaration says (Particularily, on AI companies training with the users work, or the results published with no bibliography and no account of how the result was even found) some parts of it strike me as pure panic.

None of it is an adaptation to what the future holds, but a way of advocating the past for people whose status depends on it. It says so explicitly.

"may disturb the current system of incentives"

There is no rule, but a tradition that is now being broken, that academia or the publishing community owns science, priority, credit or discoveries. In the 19th century it all worked very differently. The current system as it exists is mostly a cold war holdout.

Very few of that declaration talks of what people that are currently studying mathematics should do, a lot of it is about what it means for the ones currently holding the chair.

In a way, it is almost as if the chase for the result was valued more than the result.

It is now a fact that AI can reason as well as a trained mathematician as otherwise the Navier - Stokes result (even accounting for the controversy) would have not been possible.

So advocating for the right to not use AI, that is, to keep coding, deriving, and writing all of this entirely manually, is like advocating for astronomers to keep the right of doing all of their work looking manually through the telescope.

The tension with this idea is that, if the technology is as capable as the Navier–Stokes claim suggests, "you may abstain" will be a formality unless the academia goes full ludite and bans AI use altogether, which will mean research will keep migrating to private companies which mostly, never publish anything.

That being said, I do not think that AI replaces understanding completely, but that we need to change the way that understanding is taught, if we are to compatibilize the capabilities of the tool with the knowledge of the people using it. Of course that is the last thing a lot of people want and that tension can be felt in the letter.

How can we improve the ability of people to understand a 200-page proof or the mechanisms the AI proposes, while using AI openly and to its full capacity? That is real positive project for the future, this letter is mostly concerned with defending the institutions as they currently exist. As things currently stands, for 20 dollars, one can recruit a system that reasons as well as many fully trained people. That is just a fact, as ugly as it sounds.

I know that a lot of people will not agree with me, but it is important than instead of negation or talking of ai slop or wanting to ban ai in research altogether, a way is found to compatibilize the human understanding with the intensive use of ai. The faster they abandon this route (that is frankly modest compared to some of the AI luddites one can find on the internet), the less messy will that process be.

Sebastián Rodrigo said:

some parts of it strike me as pure panic

In the comment attached to my signature I do not imply that I want the right to not use LLMs at all (I myself have used Aristotle). Instead I want the community to integrate LLMs into their work as they have done with the many, many other computer tools that have been created over the years: SymPy, Mathematica, arb, SageMath, Cremona's mwrank, etc.

LLMs are the most powerful tools among this lot, because they can call upon all prior tools in their reasoning. Hence their immense value. But this does not mean they are deities.

My vision for the human/LLM relationship in mathematics is:

  • The paper becomes Lean-backed, with code as readable as the paper.
  • The notion of a textbook gets conflated with that of a paper, because of the readable Lean.
  • The human role is to transform the LLM's output (informal or Lean) into an efficient, reusable style of their own, so that other humans can understand the informal and LLMs can better use the Lean.
  • The LLMs (and the prior tools they call) flesh out human prompts into Tau Ceti-level proofs – true but not yet human-friendly, reusable or efficient.

The recent end-to-end FLT and Navier–Stokes formalisations are like unpolished diamonds. They can be so much more. But LLMs by themselves will not get the formalisations to that high state; human direction will be needed.

Also, there has never been a barrier to listing computers as authors on a paper. (Remember Shalosh B. Ekhad?)
